items.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: How about just once we put on Count Basie and played him just as loud? That’s my dream actually is when the other car pulls up with the loud music that I just hit “April in Paris” on my CD player

ctx.x: What’s your feeling about the marketing today of pop music and MTV? Does it strike you one way or the other, about what kids are exposed to?

Yeah I mean I still think that honestly, there’s room for a variety show of some sort. I don’t think it all has to be about 18 to 35. Because 18 or 49 can do the same thing, can coexist. And I think when you look at the early “Saturday Night Lives” they had Miles Davis and they had Preservation Hall Jazz Band and they had Wynton Marsalis, and they were eclectic. They brought just as much rock & roll as they did jazz or folk or whatever. And I think that’s the part of what that statement is about too, and I think…
If we came back and did an interview in 15 years from now, have you got goals you hope to accomplish that you can define? Or is it just keep making the best records you can?

items.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And my thing was more Bucky Pizzarelli led me down a Bucky Pizzarelli path. There was Benny Goodman, Count Basie, and Zoot Sims was our guy. So you know I was very loyal to the circle.

ctx.x: I know who you’re talking about. At least two or three people, yes.

And so you know that kind of thing, but I mean the good news is is there’s a lot of great music out there. There’s a lot of kids who now can learn in high school and in college from real live great teachers of jazz. I mean a guy like Isaiah, they — you know Isaiah and Mike, and Mike’s a product of the New School I think, too. And Isaiah out of Juilliard. And they’ll sit and they’ll sing choruses on these records they listen to. I make it sound like these records they listen to — but they’re so immersed in it. And…

mentioned that Sebesky record a number of times in other interviews I was looking at today. And Sebesky was a big part of my life in the ‘90s and well just from the ‘90s all the way ‘til his passing. You know somebody like Don Sebesky, you know, writing these arrangements and then you start to see how he harmonizes stuff and you go oh yeah that was cool. So when you start to write the chords out for somebody you go what would Don have done here? You know that was a gift.
